question: A box contains five cards, numbered \(1,\) \(2,\) \(3,\) \(4,\) and \(5.\) Three cards are selected randomly without replacement from the box. What is the probability that \(4\) is the largest value selected?
solution:
Since only the largest card matters, we can list each selection in increasing order. The possible selections are
\[
\begin{gathered}
(1,2,3),\ (1,2,4),\ (1,2,5),\ (1,3,4),\ (1,3,5),\ (1,4,5),\\
(2,3,4),\ (2,3,5),\ (2,4,5),\ (3,4,5).
\end{gathered}
\]
This list is exhaustive: it groups selections by their smallest card, which can only be \(1\), \(2\), or \(3\). Writing the cards in increasing order prevents counting the same selection twice. These ten selections are equally likely because each can be drawn in the same six orders, and every ordered draw has the same probability.

For \(4\) to be the largest card, we must select \(4\), exclude \(5\), and choose two cards from \(1,2,3\). The favorable selections are \((1,2,4)\), \((1,3,4)\), and \((2,3,4)\). Thus the probability is
\[
\frac{\text{favorable selections}}{\text{all selections}}=\frac{3}{10},
\]
which is choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
